Power & utilities · Malawi

Structures and vegetation inside Malawian power-line wayleaves, mapped and dated

The Electricity Act lets a licensee ask for a structure built in its wayleave after the line to be removed or adjusted, and take the matter to the energy regulator if that fails. AfriScan measures each structure’s distance to your line and to the wayleave edge you give us, groups them by 500 m segment and shows which are new since the last survey or the census. A person reviews every result.

Send the line KML and wayleave width See sample outputs

The problem, in your words

Wayleaves fill up between patrols

“Houses and gardens keep appearing under the line.”

The national utility’s November 2025 campaign in the Southern Region targeted rising wayleave encroachment and urged people not to build or farm under power lines. Each new structure is a safety concern, an access problem for maintenance and a harder conversation once someone lives in it.

“The new line was clear at the census.”

The census for the Malawian section of a recent 400 kV line from Mozambique ran in April and May 2019 and covered the people in its 55 m wayleave. The line was energised in August 2026. What was recorded then needs checking now, and again after each season.

“Our officers cannot reach every span in time.”

Lines cross farmland, trading centres, hills and river crossings far from a depot. What changed since the last visit is often found by a maintenance crew that cannot get to a pole.

“Poles and conductors go missing.”

Imagery cannot see theft or vandalism. It can show new tracks, cleared ground and fresh digging beside the line, which tells a patrol where to go first.

Who this is for

  • Wayleave and line-maintenance officers
  • Vegetation and bush-clearing supervisors
  • Land and resettlement teams
  • ESIA and RAP consultants
  • Teams planning new lines and interconnectors
  • Lenders’ environmental and social supervisors

The Electricity Act

What the law says about building in a wayleave

Part VIII of the Electricity Act (Cap. 73:01), “Rights over land”, gives a licensee rights over land for its lines.

  • Section 39, wayleaves over land. A licensee may place lines over land. Where consent is unreasonably withheld, the energy regulator, MERA, may consent instead and set compensation “by way of payment of a lump sum or an annual rental”.
  • Section 41, trees and structures. Trees or undergrowth that obstruct a line may be cut or trimmed after “not less than fourteen days’ notice”. “Except with the permission of the licensee, no person shall erect any building or structure in the wayleave.” For a structure put up after the line was built, “the licensee may request such a person to remove or adjust” it and, if the person does not, “may apply to the Authority for an order for the removal or adjustment”.

Two facts therefore matter for each structure: where it stands against the wayleave, and whether it was there before the line. A register measured to the wayleave edge answers the first. For the second, the register’s imagery dates, compared with scenes from before construction where the archive has them, give your wayleave officers and, where it comes to that, MERA a dated record to work from.

Check the amendment

An Electricity (Amendment) Act was published on 31 May 2024. Its commencement and its effect on sections 39 and 41 were not confirmed for this page, so check them with your counsel. This page summarises public rules for information, as read on 27 September 2026. It is not legal advice.

  • Electricity Act Cap. 73:01, consolidated text · 31 December 2017Wayleaves over land (s.39); trees, buildings and structures in the wayleave (s.41).
  • Electricity (Amendment) Act 2024 Act No. 19 of 2024 · 31 May 2024Published 31 May 2024. Its commencement and its effect on ss.39 and 41 were not confirmed for these pages.

Existing lines

A register of the wayleave, segment by segment, then what changed

We buffer the line you supply at the wayleave width for each section and list each structure the review confirms, with its distance to the line, its distance to the wayleave edge, its chainage and its coordinates. Each 500 m segment is rated high, medium or low for encroachment density by a count rule, so officers know which stretches to visit first. The rating is not a safety or clearance rating.

Engagement campaigns work best when they come with a map of where the new structures are. Because the register is sorted by segment and chainage, it can be read against the Traditional Authority and Group Village Head areas you work with, so each meeting starts from that area’s own list.

After the baseline, the line is re-surveyed on a schedule agreed with you. New and removed structures are flagged automatically and confirmed by a reviewer, with before-and-after views, and your team receives a notice after each survey. New tracks, cleared ground and fresh digging near poles and towers are flagged the same way, for a check on the ground. Around the substations you name, the line becomes a boundary: we list what stands inside the site and in a ring around it.

What you receive

  • A wayleave register: ID, distance to the line and to the wayleave edge, chainage, coordinates
  • An encroachment-density rating for each 500 m segment, with the segments ranked
  • Structures inside and around the substations you name
  • New and removed structures since the last survey, with before-and-after views
  • A notice after each re-survey
  • New tracks, cleared ground and fresh excavation near the line, for checking
  • A PDF report, GIS layers (GeoPackage, GeoJSON, KMZ, Shapefile) and an interactive map file

New lines and interconnectors

Count the homes on each route, then fix the census baseline

A 400 kV interconnector from Mozambique was energised in August 2026, and interconnectors to Zambia and to Tanzania are at feasibility stage while the grid inside the country is reinforced. Each new line needs a route, a wayleave and a resettlement plan.

Resettlement plans for new lines census the households, structures and trees in the wayleave. We compare the structures along each route option within the same widths, so the choice can weigh the land it affects. Once the route is fixed, we produce the structure layer as a reviewed, dated GIS file that the census team can start from and that later surveys are compared with. It supports the census and asset inventory; it does not replace them.

Between the census and energisation, years can pass. For the recent 400 kV line the census ran in April and May 2019 and the line was energised in August 2026; a comparison against the cut-off-date layer shows what has appeared in the wayleave since.

Lines that cross the border continue into Mozambique, where the servitude rules differ: see power lines in Mozambique.

For a new line

  • Structure counts along each route option, within the same widths
  • Steep and erosion-prone stretches screened from elevation data, and ground seen flooded in past satellite records
  • A reviewed, dated structure layer for the census team
  • New structures since the cut-off date, during compensation and construction

Vegetation

Where trees are not allowed, show where they are growing

Regrowth in the wayleave

Maps of where vegetation in the wayleave has been cleared or has grown back between dates, from Copernicus Sentinel data. They show larger patches of change, not individual trees.

Tall vegetation

Where tall vegetation stands inside the wayleave, from drone elevation models where flown and open canopy-height data for wider context. The open data is older in places, so a drone survey gives the current picture. It is not a measured clearance to conductors.

Planning the clearing notices

Section 41 lets a licensee cut or trim obstructing trees after at least fourteen days’ notice, and the resettlement plan for the recent 400 kV line allows no trees in its wayleave. A map of where the regrowth is helps plan the notices and the crews, stretch by stretch.

How it works

From line file to reviewed wayleave register

  1. Agree the widths

    You send the line, pole or tower positions if you have them, the voltage, the wayleave width for each section and what the register is for. The written proposal fixes the widths, the imagery and the deliverables.

  2. Screen the whole line

    Structures are mapped along the full length from dated satellite imagery, open building datasets or imagery you already hold, with no flight over the line.

  3. Add detail where it is needed

    Spans that need a closer look are flown by drone, subject to the approvals and security clearances each job requires, with the Surveyor General’s 30-day notice built into the plan.

  4. Review, measure and deliver

    A person checks every result. Each structure is measured to the line and the wayleave edge, each segment is rated, and the files go to the contacts you name.

Honest scope

What we do, and what we don’t

What we do

  • Map structures, cleared ground, fresh excavations, tracks and vegetation change visible from the air
  • Measure each structure to the line and to the wayleave edge you give us
  • Flag change between dated surveys, confirmed by a reviewer
  • Deliver dated records that support your engagement, compensation, legal and community processes

What we don’t do

  • Measure conductor clearances or inspect poles, towers and hardware
  • Detect theft or vandalism, or identify who did anything
  • Identify, count or follow people
  • Prepare records for evictions, or decide whether a structure may stay

Frequently asked questions

What wayleave width do you measure to?

The width for each line or section, which you give us. The only width we quote from a published document is the 55 m wayleave of a recent 400 kV line from Mozambique. We quote no standard width for 11, 33, 66 or 132 kV lines, so send yours, or the wayleave polygons from your GIS. We report each structure’s distance to the line and to the wayleave edge, and a band beyond it where you want one, with up to six widths in one survey.

Can the licensee have a structure in the wayleave removed?

Section 41 of the Electricity Act says no one may put up a building or structure in the wayleave without the licensee’s permission. For a structure built after the line, the licensee may ask for it to be removed or adjusted and, if that fails, apply to MERA for an order. Whether a particular structure predates the line, or had permission, is for your legal team and MERA. The register records the imagery date on which each structure was mapped and, where earlier scenes exist, when it first appears.

Do you measure clearance to conductors?

No. We show where structures and tall vegetation stand in the wayleave and how far each structure is from the line. Tall vegetation comes from drone elevation models where flown and from open canopy-height data, which is older in places. None of it is a measured clearance, which stays with your line engineers.

Can you detect vandalism, or stolen conductors and poles?

No. Satellites cannot see theft or vandalism. We flag new tracks, cleared ground, fresh excavations and structures near the line between surveys, so your wayleave officers can target their patrols.

Can the register be taken to meetings with Traditional Authorities?

That is your decision. The register lists structures by segment and chainage, with no names, so it can help plan engagement with each Traditional Authority and Group Village Head along the line. Imagery of homes can still be personal data under the Data Protection Act 2024, so agree how it is shared before it leaves your team.

Can a drone fly along the line?

Only under a written authorisation from the Malawi Civil Aviation Authority, after 30 days’ notice of the aerial survey to the Surveyor General, and with a drone registered with the Surveyor General for survey work. No statutory drone distance from lines or substations is published, so flights keep well clear of energised conductors and work under the site owner’s permit to work. See drone law in Malawi.

Send the line KML and the wayleave width

KML, KMZ, GeoJSON, Shapefile, GPX or GeoPackage, or the pole and tower coordinates, with the voltage, the wayleave width for each section and the districts it crosses. Tell us what the register is for: maintenance, an engagement campaign, a new line or a census baseline. We reply with a scope, an imagery plan and a written proposal.
